summary:
Red Atlas is an edge-native Martian navigation system engineered to equip future Martians with the knowledge of their environment and help in Mission activities. At its core, the platform introduces two breakthrough capabilities: real-time 3D Gaussian-Splat terrain reconstruction and a contactless spacesuit helmet heads-up display (HUD).

While there are traditional mapping tools, we are addressing the severe distortion and needle-like spikes typical of traditional polygon elevation meshes, Red Atlas renders orbital NASA MOLA and HiRISE data as surface-normal-aligned 3D Gaussian splats. This achieves continuous, sub-meter photorealistic terrain at 60+ FPS on field hardware, enabling instantaneous hazard slope probing. Concurrently, because stiff 29.6 kPa pressurized spacesuit gloves prevent touchscreen usage, we developed an optical vision HUD driven by helmet-mounted cameras and lightweight MediaPipe AI. Astronauts effortlessly navigate multi-spectral orbital maps, inspect minerals via synthetic reticles, and monitor dynamic Points of Safe Return (PSR) using intuitive touchless glove micro-gestures.

Red Atlas is vital because human explorers cannot wait twenty minutes for Earth during critical extravehicular emergencies. By fusing high-fidelity Gaussian splatting with intuitive visor avionics, Red Atlas equips astronauts with the immediate autonomy needed to safely explore, plan, and survive on Mars
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Red Atlas is a complete tactical mapping and spacesuit navigation platform designed for astronauts during Martian Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). It operates across a 4-tier pipeline:

  • Data Ingestion: Streams multi-resolution orbital tiles directly from NASA JPL Mars Trek and core scientific archives (MRO HiRISE for 0.25 m/px imagery, MGS MOLA for laser topography, Odyssey THEMIS for thermal inertia regolith firmness, and MRO CRISM/SHARAD for hydrated minerals and subsurface ice).
  • Intelligence Core: Aligns all datasets onto the IAU Mars 2000 planetary coordinate datum. A three-pass filter removes digital elevation model (DEM) artifact spikes. An autonomous routing engine integrates distance, slope hazards (>15∘), and surface softness into a cost function while continuously monitoring life-support consumables (oxygen/power) to establish an unbreakable Point of Safe Return (PSR) boundary.
  • 3D Gaussian-Splat Terrain: Bypasses distorted polygon meshes by rendering terrain using surface-normal-aligned 3D Gaussian ellipsoids (Σ=RSSTRT\Sigma = R S S^T R^TΣ=RSSTRT) via screen-space Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) projection, delivering continuous, spike-free 60+ FPS photorealism.
  • Twin Operational Interfaces: Simultaneously feeds a desktop Mission-Control Dashboard for base habitat planners and an Augmented Reality Helmet HUD inside the spacesuit visor, controlled completely hands-free via optical glove tracking.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Instantaneous Tactical Autonomy: Eliminates life-threatening reliance on Earth’s 4 to 24-minute one-way radio latency during sudden EVA emergencies.
  • Preserves Astronaut Stamina (Zero Glove Fatigue): Pressurized EVA suits (inflated to 29.6 kPa) make bending fingers feel like squeezing a tennis ball. Touchless optical gesture recognition eliminates the physical strain of tapping tablets or screens.
  • Artifact-Free Hazard Detection: Standard polygon meshes create artificial "needle spikes" kilometres tall from corrupted elevation pixels and stretch textures on cliffs. Gaussian splatting maintains true physical slope geometry, allowing instant surface raycasting to determine ground steepness.
  • Dynamic Consumables Safety Margin: Rather than estimating return times with simple linear distance, the PSR dynamically recalculates walking vs. rover pace, uphill metabolic burn, and a mandatory 25% safety reserve.

3. What is the intended impact of our project?

The intended impact is to bridge the historical gap between static planetary science archives on Earth and dynamic human survival on Mars. Today, thirty years of rich NASA remote sensing data remains isolated in massive, siloed databases accessed via desktop GIS by Earth-bound scientists. Red Atlas transforms this orbital data into an active, life-saving field avionics tool. By equipping the first human explorers with immediate, intuitive, and hands-free situational awareness, Red Atlas significantly lowers mission risk, maximizes scientific discovery per EVA sol, and helps pave the way for permanent, sustainable interplanetary settlement.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

  • Languages & Frameworks: JavaScript (ES6+), React 18, Vite 5, HTML5/CSS3, Python 3.13, GLSL Shaders.
  • 3D & Mapping Engines: Three.js (r160+) for the tilted 3D planetary globe and custom Gaussian splat point-cloud shaders; Leaflet 1.9 for 2D level-of-detail GIS tiles; NASA JPL Mars Trek WMTS API.
  • Computer Vision & AI: Google MediaPipe Tasks Vision (hand_landmarker.task), LiteRT / TensorFlow Lite with XNNPACK CPU acceleration, OpenCV (cv2), PyGrabber (Windows COM DirectShow Graph engine), and a trained Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) for 42D normalized gesture classification.
  • Hardware: Logitech Brio 4K / C270 UVC camera hardware, simulated helmet AR visor optical display, and multi-core edge processor targets (sub-15 ms latency, no heavy CUDA GPU required).

5. How is our project creative?

  • First Application of 3D Gaussian Splatting to Planetary GIS: Instead of using Gaussian Splatting merely for artistic rendering, we adapted principles from the ESGS remote sensing framework, anchoring splat covariances to orbital surface normals to solve elevation data corruption.
  • Glove-Invariant 42D Kinematics: Standard vision models fail when hands are covered by bulky spacesuit gloves. We engineered a scale- and position-invariant 42D vector normalizer relative to the wrist, making gestures like micro-pinches and dual-fist proximity completely independent of glove thickness or camera distance.
  • Thermal-Inertia-Aware Routing: While typical GPS algorithms only compute shortest physical distance, Red Atlas combines MOLA slope with THEMIS thermal inertia to differentiate between safe, firm basaltic bedrock and treacherous, wheel-sinking fine dust.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  • Martian Physics & Lighting: Mars's 25.19∘ axial tilt, atmospheric Rayleigh rim scattering, extreme shadow-to-glare contrast dynamic range, and the 15° vehicle/suit rollover hazard threshold.
  • Human Physiology & Spacesuit Mechanics: Space suit glove stiffness (29.6 kPa pressure differential), metabolic O2 consumption spikes when traversing steep inclines, and the cognitive load on astronauts in low-visibility dust storms.
  • Computing & Communications Realities: Extreme Earth-Mars latency (up to 24 min), field hardware constraints (low electrical wattage, absence of power-hungry desktop GPUs on EVA suits), requiring XNNPACK CPU optimizations and lightweight Float32 GPU buffers.
